why.support: A good review is an opinion **with reasons**. It says what is good, what is not, and who will like it. Then people trust you.
why.core: A good review is an opinion **with reasons**. It tells people what's good, what's not, and who'll like it. Write reviews like that and people trust you — whether it's a game, a film or a café.
why.extend: A strong review is a short piece of evaluation: a clear judgement, backed by specific evidence, using precise language about how the text works. It's the same skill you'll use to argue a point at work or justify a decision.

articles.title: What makes a review worth reading

body.support:
A **review** says how good something is and **why**. It could be a film, a game, a song or a café.

A good review gives **reasons**:

- *It's boring.* (No reason. Not helpful.)
- *It's boring because the middle is slow.* (Better.)
- *It's boring because the middle is slow. Nothing happens for 20 minutes.* (Best!)

Use critic words: **plot**, **character**, **setting**, **music**.

A review has a shape:

1. **Verdict** — your rating.
2. **What it's about** — no spoilers!
3. **The good.**
4. **The not so good.**
5. **Who will like it.**

Be **honest**. If everything gets 5 stars, stars mean nothing.
body.core:
A **review** is a short piece of writing that judges something — a film, game, song, book or café — and says **why**.

The big difference between a useless review and a good one is **reasons**:

- **Bare opinion:** *It's boring.*
- **Opinion + reason:** *It's boring because the middle drags.*
- **Opinion + reason + example:** *It's boring because the middle drags — there's a 20-minute training montage where nothing happens.*

Critics use **precise words** about how the text works: **plot**, **character**, **setting**, **pacing**, **soundtrack**, **visuals** or, for games, **gameplay** and **controls**.

Most reviews follow the same shape:

1. **Verdict** — your overall judgement, up front.
2. **What it's about** — a quick summary, with **no spoilers**.
3. **The good** — with examples.
4. **The not so good** — be fair.
5. **Who it's for** — *If you liked…, you'll like this.*

The best reviews are **honest**. If everything gets five stars, the stars mean nothing.
body.extend:
A **review** is a short piece of evaluation. It makes a judgement about a work and **backs it up** with evidence.

The gap between a throwaway comment and a useful review is the backing:

- **Bare claim:** *It's boring.*
- **Claim + reason:** *It's boring because the middle drags.*
- **Claim + reason + evidence:** *The middle drags. A twenty-minute training montage adds nothing to the plot or the characters.*

Critics use **metalanguage**: exact words for how a text works, like **plot**, **character**, **setting**, **pacing**, **tone**, **soundtrack**, or **gameplay** for games. Judging words (*gripping*, *clumsy*, *forgettable*) only convince when an example backs them up.

Most reviews follow the same shape: verdict, a summary with no spoilers, strengths, weaknesses, and who it's for.

Above all, a review is a promise of honesty. When reviews are faked or filtered, every reader is misled.

caseStudies.title: The reviews that went missing

body.support:
**Meriton** runs apartments for travellers. After a stay, a website called **TripAdvisor** emailed guests to ask for a review.

For almost a year, Meriton staff hid the emails of guests who might write a **bad review**. Those guests never got asked. So only the happy guests wrote reviews.

The **ACCC** looks out for shoppers. It took Meriton to court. In **2018**, the court made Meriton pay **$3 million**.

Why? People trusted the reviews. But the reviews didn't show the whole truth.
body.core:
**Meriton** is a big Australian company that runs serviced apartments. After guests stayed, **TripAdvisor** emailed them asking for a review.

From **November 2014 to October 2015**, Meriton staff changed or hid the email addresses of guests they thought might leave a **bad review**. So those guests never got the email, and never wrote the review. The good reviews kept coming.

The **ACCC**, which protects shoppers, took Meriton to court. The court found Meriton had misled people. In **2018** it ordered Meriton to pay **$3 million**.

Why does it matter? People booked rooms trusting the reviews. But the reviews didn't show the full picture.
body.extend:
**Meriton**, a major Australian property company, operates serviced apartments. After each stay, **TripAdvisor** emailed guests inviting them to post a review.

From **November 2014 to October 2015**, Meriton staff changed or hid the email addresses of guests they thought would complain. Those guests never got the invitation. Good reviews kept coming; bad ones were quietly filtered out.

The **ACCC** took the case to the Federal Court, which found Meriton had misled people. In **2018** Meriton was ordered to pay **$3 million** in penalties, and was barred from filtering the guest emails it sent to TripAdvisor for three years. The ACCC called it a first-of-its-kind case.

No review was faked, yet readers were still misled. Honesty in reviews isn't only about what's written. It's also about whose voices get heard.

teacher.overview: Students learn that a review is an evaluative text: a verdict substantiated by reasons and examples, using metalanguage about plot, character, pacing and sound. They upgrade bare opinions, annotate a review's structure, and write their own review of a text they know well. The case study is the ACCC's $3 million case against Meriton for filtering who could post TripAdvisor reviews.
prep: Collect 2–3 short real reviews (film, game, food) at different quality levels. Rotten Tomatoes snippets or Google reviews work well.
Check students' choices of text to review are school-appropriate.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Opinions with reasons
steps: **Hook (10 min):** show a useless review and a useful one for the same thing. Which would you trust?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** opinion → reason → example; critic words.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Shape and honesty
steps: **Upgrade (15 min):** model one aloud, then pairs.
**Case study (20 min):** Meriton; discuss whether online reviews can be trusted.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Write it
steps: **Write (25 min):** final mission. Option: read reviews aloud in pairs.
**Level Up (10 min):** compare with a professional review.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** Worst movie ever — bare; jokes land because… — backed; burger huge but bun soggy — backed; song slaps — bare; open world/map — backed; everyone should watch — bare.

**Review annotation:** 1 verdict; 2 spoiler-free summary; 3 strength with reason (silence → tension); 4 weakness; 5 audience/recommendation; 6 rating.

**Case study:** staff masked emails of guests likely to complain, so they weren't invited to review; readers saw a filtered, overly positive picture, so they were misled even though no review was fake.

realityCheck: **Students love this one.** It's their own taste, and every student has something they're an expert in. That makes it a strong starter for reluctant writers.
**Watch the choice of text.** Some students will pick M or R-rated films or games. Decide your rule in advance, e.g. it must be OK to talk about in class.

**The literary codes are real, but light.** It counts as responding to literary texts if they review a film, show, game story, song or book. A café review practises the skills but is weaker evidence for the Literature codes, so steer students towards a text.
**The case study is about businesses, not teens.** It connects well if you open with “have you ever trusted reviews to pick something?”
**Works in a real class:** yes, with almost no prep. Reading reviews aloud in pairs is a quick, low-stakes speaking task too.
